This is the Daggerford map help.

Just click on something! :)

Welcome to the world map!

For those of you familiar with the Baldur's Gate world map system, this world map works just the same. The world map will appear when you leave an area, so you can decide which area you want to travel to next.

Each area is represented by an icon on the world map. Most of these area icons are "hidden" and invisible at the start of the game. You must explore the many areas of the world to uncover new icons on the map. Once you have visited an area, the icon for that area becomes "visible." Visible icons appear in color on the map, and you can always quickly and easily travel to any of these known locales from any other area on the map.

When you leave an area, you may uncover a hidden adjoining area. The icon for this area will then be "revealed." Revealed icons appear as gray and flashing on the map. You must travel to revealed areas directly, by entering that area from an adjoining area's connecting exit. For example, if a revealed icon appears to the west of a visible icon (i.e., your current area), you may only reach this revealed area by traveling via your current area's western exit.

NPCs may reveal hidden areas by marking them on your map for you. If you wish to reach a distant area revealed by an NPC, then you must travel in that direction, adventuring through the areas that lie between.

We hope these instructions will help you in your travels!

Stinky Beef Stew

Ingredients:

1 dead cow plus entrails
1 bunch black mold
1 handful mushrooms
7 pints beer
7 pints scrumpy cider
Some kind of thorny bush

Directions:

1. Chop up dead cow in four pieces.
2. Wrap some entrails around each cow piece and fasten tight with toothpick.
3. Hold cow piece over fire until eyes water from stink.
4. Chop up burnt cow and entrails and put bits in pot.
5. Drink one pint of beer and pour one pint of scrumpy cider into pot. Do this until all beer and cider is gone.
6. Put pot on fire.
7. Drop in mold, mushrooms, and thorny bush.
8. Cook until stew so burnt it stink up kitchen.
9. Serve with lemon wedge and sprig of parsley.

Illefarn

Hear ye all my tale of woe,
About the land called Illefarn,
Which bordered on the elven lands,
And sheltered all from pain and harm.

Welcoming was the elven lord,
And gracious was his lady fair,
With gates set wide to visiting kings,
And pleasantries exchanged without a care.

Then came humans on shining mounts,
To hoe and farm the blackened soil,
Met kindly by elves and dwarves alike,
They reaped the bounty of endless toil.

But kinship was lost to orcish hordes,
Come down from the north with axe and shield,
Who destroyed the ranks of elves and dwarves,
And slew all humans too brave to yield.

Now but a shadow of its former glory,
Wondrous Illefarn has fallen away,
But lest ye lose hope of great Illefarn's revival,
Know that we dwarves will yet have our day.

History of Daggerford

Daggerford was founded along the Trade Way, at the major crossing of the River Delimbiyr south of Waterdeep. The settlement has stood for nearly 400 years and now consists of about 40 stone buildings and a castle, all protected by a high stone wall.

The town of Daggerford gets its name from a historic altercation between a merchant's son and a lizardfolk raiding party. The young man, armed only with a dagger, stood in the middle of the ford and held off the lizardfolk until reinforcements could arrive.

The Greatshouts are the ruling family of Daggerford with Duke Pwyll Greatshout being the town's current leader. The Greatshouts have ruled Daggerford for five generations, dating back to the first Duke, Rugyar the Just.

Daggerford is viewed by many as a backwater, especially when compared to Waterdeep, the town's nearest neighbor. It is not uncommon for Waterdhavian criminals and corrupt politicians to set up temporary roots in Daggerford, until their troubles in Waterdeep blow over. For this reason, Daggerford's population is more diverse and cultured than the typical agrarian town along the Trade Way.

Beware the Lizard Marsh!
Another expeditionary tale of infamous Sword Coast locales, by Emythene Faldree and her renowned group of crack adventurers.
* * *

This time, dear readers, we shall be exploring the Lizard Marsh to the west of the town of Daggerford, just along the coast. Historically an unpleasant place, the Lizardfolk within the marsh have always been an ever-present threat to Daggerford, the Trade Way traffic, and not to mention the local farmers themselves. The name Daggerford is in fact derived from a boy who wielded a mere dagger to defend himself against a score of Lizardfolk on the banks of the River Delimbiyr several centuries ago. But the mysteries of the marsh have remained largely undiscovered since that time. So let us proceed and see exactly what secrets the Lizard Marsh holds...
- Emythene Faldree

Day 3. The dark branches seem to reach at us like clawed hands as we trekked through the quagmire of the marsh, with the mud sucking at our boots. After our initial encounter with the feral tribal Lizardfolk, our show of force seems to have dissuaded them from continued probing of our defenses. Our tracker guide insists though that they are shadowing our progress, and he can constantly be seen staring into the dark green waters after the elusive creatures.

Day 4. We have been lucky. A black dragon, obviously quite young judging from its size, took us by surprise today. It burst from the trees with such ferocity that it made quick work of one of our porters before we could move to defend ourselves. The creature did not escape with its prize, however, as our arrows had feathered it before it could take many steps back towards its refuge. We pried out its razor-sharp teeth as souvenirs, for how many can claim to have slain a dragon!

Day 6. We have lost Durns. A snake so small as to be beneath notice has turned out to be highly poisonous. Durns' joviality will be missed around the nightly fires.

Day 7. We have been faced with several attacks from the Lizardfolk and these assaults have not left us unscathed. Three of our guards now lie dead, including dear Ignatious. I am beginning to believe that these attacks are only meant to wear us down and not true offensives. The marsh itself wears on our morale as well.

Day 9. It looked as if the Lizardfolk had finally decided to leave us be, disappearing completely into the foliage, but the reason became clear before long. In a brackish pond along which we made camp, we encountered a beast undoubtedly related to the common turtle found in many creeks. Yet the size and viciousness of this beast was of a completely different scale. Four members of our group are dead or dying from wounds caused by its huge snapping jaws after they strolled along the pond's edge. I am loath to leave behind the prize of its shell, which is a full 14 feet across and thick enough to stop arrows. Instead, its massive head is the prize I shall return with.

Day 10. A dark form in the night took the last porter. Sharp claws riding upon leathery wings by the sole account of it. I am forced to abandon my prize as only four of us remain.

Day 11. Our guide has abandoned us. Curse him!

Day 12. Maltan, Kegrunt, and I have decided that our expedition is unfortunately at an end. We shall navigate back towards Daggerford using the sun by day and the stars by night, just as we did when we became lost at sea in search of the Isle of Mysts. Although we leave this adventure behind us, we shall live to see another day and more adventures along the Sword Coast! We may not have uncovered all the mysteries within the marsh, but we have confirmed that its dangers are quite vicious, and that it is indeed a most inhospitable place. To all those who would dare to venture here, all I can counsel is this: beware the Lizard Marsh!

Trade Way Travel Stops: A Visitor's Guide to the Trade Way South of Daggerford

So, you've seen all there is to see of the quaint, country town known as Daggerford and are at a loss for what to do next. Well, my friends, the Trade Way area south of Daggerford is an area literally brimming with the promise of new adventures.

Leaving Daggerford by its Caravan Gate and heading south for half a day, your first stop is Gillian's Hill, a charming hamlet that once served as the center of law enforcement along this stretch of the Trade Way. Today, the small outpost serves as a minor trading hub and includes an excellent curiosity shop known as Torleth's Treasures. Other places of note include the historical Gillian's Hill Cemetery and the famed Gillian's Tower that served as a lookout post for the hamlet's namesake and former ranger-protector, Gillian Cantilar.

Another half-day's journey past Gillian's Hill lies Liam's Hold. This is a fine place to book a room for the night. Although the hamlet lies not far from the treacherous Trollbark Forest, the area is well-protected (for the most part), and the Holdfast Inn offers soft beds and lively conversation. You may find some of the Liam's Hold locals to be a tad superstitious, but this only serves to heighten the burg's old-world, agrarian atmosphere.

South of Liam's Hold, it is best to hire onto a caravan, as much for your protection as theirs...

This colossal shield was unearthed from a tomb in the shifting sands of the Anauroch desert. The thief who uncovered the tomb attributed the shield's magical properties to his escape from the desert's punishing heat. Feeling emboldened by the shield's powers, the thief returned to the desert, this time with a small army of bloodthirsty brigands. He used this band to raid passing caravans for months until he was finally hunted down and killed, close to the same tomb from which he obtained the shield.

Lord Francis Tenraw commissioned this suit of armor in anticipation of a war that never came. The suit served him well in a ceremonial fashion, until his death (of old age). His daughter, who did not see the use of ceremony, sold the armor to finance a library.

This axe was created for the mighty dwarven chief known as King Taik. The weapon's sole purpose was to keep at bay the orcish hordes that continuously threatened Taik's subterranean realm. It was forged with the blood of the orcish sorcerer Sajifot, and inherited some of that spellcaster's bloodthirsty nature.

Blood Frenzy is best known for cutting off the head of Kumon, the leader of an orcish horde, thus breaking the horde's morale and causing their eventual extinction. The axe was buried with King Taik in a secret tomb and is believed lost for all time.

Created by a gnomish bowyer, this weapon was crafted from the heartwood of a treant and strung with hairs from the tail of a unicorn. The gnome was so impressed with his handiwork that he planned an elaborate exhibition for his fellow gnomes and anyone else in the area who wished to attend.

The performance consisted of the bowyer firing crossbow bolts at long range into water-filled barrels. Each time a bolt struck a barrel, the container literally exploded into bits, splashing the crowd of cheering onlookers. However, one particular onlooker, a half-orc bounty hunter, was not particularly amused or impressed.

This bounty hunter followed the bowyer back to his home and, with one strike from her hand axe, summarily ended the gnome's budding career as an entertainer. The bounty hunter also claimed the crossbow for her own, although she wisely avoided revealing its prowess to others.

Hadrian Coltin was a procurer of rare items for Bintley's in Waterdeep. Hadrian's job often required that he "liberate" these items from their unwilling owners. This, of course, led to frequent scrapes with the owners' hired mercenaries, who guarded their masters' property with dogged determination. Eventually, Hadrian realized he needed to improve his swordplay skills if he were to remain alive.

He remembered that his father, a minor noble, had willed him a large bastard sword, called Bloody Longblade. The father's choice of weapon type was symbolic, as Hadrian's mother had been a serving wench in the local tavern. Despite the gift's hurtful intentions, Hadrian grew to value the weapon as an effective aid in prolonging his career as a collector.

History of Daggerford

Daggerford was founded along the Trade Way, at the major crossing of the River Delimbiyr south of Waterdeep. The settlement has stood for nearly 400 years and now consists of about 40 stone buildings and a castle, all protected by a high stone wall.

The town of Daggerford gets its name from a historic altercation between a merchant's son and a lizardfolk raiding party. The young man, armed only with a dagger, stood in the middle of the ford and held off the lizardfolk until reinforcements could arrive.

The Greatshouts are the ruling family of Daggerford with Duke Pwyll Greatshout being the town's current leader. The Greatshouts have ruled Daggerford for five generations, dating back to the first Duke, Rugyar the Just.

Daggerford is viewed by many as a backwater, especially when compared to Waterdeep, the town's nearest neighbor. It is not uncommon for Waterdhavian criminals and corrupt politicians to set up temporary roots in Daggerford, until their troubles in Waterdeep blow over. For this reason, Daggerford's population is more diverse and cultured than the typical agrarian town along the Trade Way.

Gravia's Hot Apple Cider

Ingredients:

1/2 gallon apple juice
2 cinnamon sticks
2 whole cloves
2 allspice berries
1/2 orange peel, cut into strips
1/2 lemon peel, cut into strips
Special ingredient (see note below)

Directions:

1. Pour apple juice into a large pot.
2. Wrap spices and peels in a thin, porous cloth.
3. Drop cloth into apple juice.
4. Heat juice to a boil and then slow cook for two hours.
5. Remove cloth.
6. Add the special ingredient.
7. Serve hot!

Note: A fellow named Stran in the Black Stone Inn sells "knockout drops," which are added to the cider immediately before presenting it to "the victim."

This rod was brought to Faerûn by an elder earth elemental, who left it in the care of a gnomish apprentice conjurer, named Elbix, explaining to him its limited power. At his settlement's local tavern, Elbix would often exaggerate to awe-struck ears the wondrous powers of his rod. It brought him a measure of respect and often several rounds of free drinks.

Several years later, he finally had occasion to use it. A great ettin chief, by the name of Gnarltooth, was fast approaching the gnomish lands, leading a gang of ettins. This prompted the gnome leader to hurriedly summon Elbix and his mighty rod to save the gnomish settlement. By this time, the conjurer's tall tales of the weapon had swollen it to legendary proportion. What made matters worse was that none of the other gnomes were bothering to prepare any defenses at all and instead pinned their expectations on the Stonestick to obliterate the monsters within minutes.

A nervous Elbix saw no hope of survival when he was left to face the oncoming creatures. Gnarltooth easily snatched up the thrashing gnome for a closer look but accidentally received the Stonestick in the eye. This caused the monster to trip backwards and, incredibly, impale itself on its own spear. With the defeat of their leader, the other ettins fled. The result was that Elbix became the luckiest gnome in the world and, intending to keep it that way, tossed the Stonestick into the river at the earliest opportunity.

The proud White Stag of Dargendale eluded poachers for decades in the Dargendale forest. This pleased the peasantry greatly, as the creature was seen as a sign of good luck when it was spotted. It was not until the day of Worlges the Black, who laid a cunning trap in the forest, that the White Stag was finally captured. Merely mounting its head upon the wall was not good enough for Worlges. He declared that he would have the creature slain and then completely stuffed from head to toe, to be kept in his personal chambers to remind him how fantastic a hunter he was. The unfortunate creature was indeed killed and stuffed as predicted, despite the angry clamor from the peasantry. What was not predicted, however, was that a traveling druid would one night sneak into Worlges chambers and temporarily bring back to life the spirit of the White Stag. The animated stuffed creature soon exacted revenge upon the sleeping man with its sharp antlers, savagely striking again and again, shredding up the bed in the process. Worlges the Black was found dead the next morning, pierced in innumerable places and, to his servants' shock, completely covered in the down stuffing from his mattress. The immobile, stuffed stag stood in the corner, staring woodenly onto the gruesome scene, and it had nothing to say. It was later jested by the peasants that it was Worlges, who in the end, "got as good a stuffing as any man could!" If you look closely, you can still see traces of blood upon the antlers.

The golden finish on this suit of armor is highly alluring. However, two things shall dissuade prospective buyers from ever contemplating purchasing it. The first is that it is not solid gold but merely gold plated (undoubtedly it was a frugal knight who originally had it commissioned). The second is that it is haunted. In much the same way that an angry resident ghost can terrorize a household, so it is with the "Haunted Armor." At one point, the armor had belonged to the benevolent King Ulther, but his treacherous and ambitious nephew, Prince Zherost, soon saw to shortening the king's reign. The night before the king was to take part in a tournament, Zherost poured a special poison all inside the suit of armor. This quickly disposed of the king the next day...almost. Somehow, the king's ghost remained within the armor. Prince Zherost did not know of this until his coronation, where he donned the golden suit to receive his crown in full style. It was later noted that the prince had become increasingly agitated as the service went on, repeatedly looking over his shoulder and above him, complaining of whispers around him. However, before he could be crowned king, he fled shrieking in terror from the hall, tugging at his armor to remove it, and in the process inadvertently tripped over the battlements and into the moat. It is a well-known fact that knights in shining armor make very poor swimmers, and so he sunk to his death. It is said that both the spirits of Ulther and Zherost now occupy the armor, forever in torment together. Anyone foolish enough to wear the Haunted Armor could very well join them.

Unfortunately, this sudden rise in riches made the young Stonehand warriors the targets of the single dwarven females of the Licehair clan. To combat this sudden rise in popularity, Kurgin Stonehand commissioned the creation of these magic belts, which lower the wearer's Charisma to depths far below even a dwarf's regrettable standards.

The sound it makes renders creatures helpless with pain and frequently causes bleeding from the ears, much like Lady Oonagh's singing.

The Brush of Barbs is so known because of its overgrown thickets of thorns that have overrun the trees and woods in the area, making trekking through the brush a very difficult endeavor. In some spots, the brush is impassable due to the volume of thorns. One such spot is the sequestered grove of the Stone Circle of Govan. Constructed by an elven druid named Govan Irfandel over 200 years ago, the stone circle of standing stones was meant to provide a meeting and ritual place for the local good-aligned druids. It was said that the trees, thickets, and vines were the ones who moved the heavy stones into place with accurate precision.

Long ago, near the ancient shores of Torslunda, an old poet dwelled alone in crumbling Daargard Keep. Each night, by flickering candlelight, the old poet labored to wrap his thoughts in ink and verse. Already blind with age, the poet felt the bitter kiss of fate, for he lived long enough to touch his beloved son's grave stone. In the dark keep, upon rows of faded scrolls, the old poet patiently scribed his stories using powerful runes of blood.

Many long years later, a noble Lord and Lady departed on an epic island adventure, and arrived upon the shores of ancient Torslunda. The Lord and Lady explored the forgotten ruins of Daargard Keep, and discovered several of the blind poet's scrolls. These treasured works of art have been passed carefully from generation to generation so that the old poet's colorful songs have entertained and inspired hundreds of hopeful adventurers across many lands.

Each of the blind poet's songs is about a different theme. This particular song is about the old poet's fear of death. When sung by a bard, the bard gains a brief mastery over death, and his nearby enemies suffer damage.

with nothing but a "twig" in his hand. Had they known what would happen next, the soldiers might have 
retracted their joke, as the entire unit was engulfed within a blazing inferno.

Why on earth would Torleth keep barrels of rocks in his shop? The large, coarse rocks with golden chunks aren't even for sale. No, not gold, but apparently fool's gold! And not just any fool's gold either. This batch was traded by a particularly unsavory dwarven merchant, to a local prima donna sculptor named Yujist Glemp. Yujist wished to create a gold casting of himself for posterity's sake, although the locals would quite disagree, saying posterity was the last thing they wanted from Yujist (the first being his posterior on the road). The sculptor, never being very good with money matters, had bought the fake gold using a loan from a Daggerford loan shark named Vladmyr, telling him that his golden statue could be used as collateral should he not be able to repay later. Fool's gold, as it turns out, makes for very poor collateral, and the fool Glemp was forced to flee in all haste from the Daggerford region. Vladmyr found nothing but barrels of the useless ore in the sculptor's abandoned studio, and stormed off fuming. Torleth, a competitor of Vladmyr's, laughed so hard at what had happened, that he had the barrels brought into his store, just so he could get a chuckle at Vladmyr's expense every once in a while.

"The Boiler," as it was commonly referred to by the Flaming Fist Company of Baldur's Gate, was a large iron cauldron used to pour boiling oil onto unwelcome invaders who attempted to scale the city's ramparts. Unfortunately, "The Boiler" often displayed the nasty habit of rocking backwards after being emptied over the wall, and splashing its operators with sizzling oil. This made it a terror among the troops. Some pronounced the contraption as lethal to the defenders as it was to the invaders, and all attempts to fix it proved fruitless. To have simply replaced it would have been the most logical solution, but doing so would have been seen as a great insult to the city, as it had been a gift to the Flaming Fists from the noble family of one of the deceased grand dukes. Sergeant Lukas Oteril, however, saw a golden opportunity during one particularly turbulent attack by an orcish horde. Having run out of oil, and faced with a swarm of snorting green orcs clambering up the wall on a crude ladder, Lukas had his troops heave "The Boiler" itself right over the edge and onto the scaling attacks below. The effect on the horde was marginal, as more of the creatures moved in to fill the fallen ranks, but the soldiers were all smiles at the outcome. The important thing was that "The Boiler" was gone for good. Nobody truly knew where it disappeared to after the battle, although it was said to have been carried off by an orc chieftain, to be used as a cooking pot back home. How it ended up in Torleth's possession though is an even greater mystery.

This simple rowboat was the vessel for a forbidden love between the young man, Patrolio, and the young woman, Galenia, who were separated by a river. Their respective families greatly disapproved of the match, but this did nothing to deter the passion that had been ignited between the two. Their first meeting in the marketplace, where their eyes had locked for but a moment, had been the spark that had started it all. The chance touch of his hand upon hers at the theatre, when they both reached for the same refreshment, became the kindling for their youthful yearning. And finally, their talk alone together outside on the balcony at the Duke's ball became the bellows that fanned the flames of desire to the highest of levels. Patrolio and Galenia decided that they had to be together; that their hearts could not bear the constant separation, and no familial wrath, no fear of societal scorn, not even the gods themselves could keep them apart any longer! "Wait for me upon the morrow's eve," Patrolio whispered to Galenia, as they parted for the last time at the Duke's ball. "Under the cover of night I shall arrive by my boat to the dock of your house, and together we shall float away upon the watery divide that once separated us." Galenia kissed him and responded in a hushed voice, "Then I shall await you, Patrolio my love. Your voice is aphrodisia to my soul, and I yearn to hear it again before long." It was never known who had overheard their conversation, be it a member of one family or the other. But it was surely the same insidious individual who drilled the hole in Patrolio's boat, causing him to be pulled down to his death in the swirling dark waters of the river. Galenia was to wait in vain and eventually wither from a broken heart, from her life's great love who had seemingly abandoned her. Theatrical troupes along the Sword Coast have recounted this tragic tale, sitting in this very boat for the drowning scene and ensuing soliloquy. It is most assuredly a replica of Patrolio's famous boat, detailed right down to the cork that has been pushed into the drilled hole in the bottom.

From the heart of the Lizard Marsh come the gourds of a giant fruit. Hollowed out and then dried to have a hard shell exterior, they are used extensively by the lizardfolk as great vessels with which to hold a variety of liquids, from fresh water, to special fermented drinks, to small swimming snacks. This gourd, however, seems to have been used for something entirely different. Carved onto the hard surface is the word "Butterfly," beside which are three straight-line marks. According to the local sea tales in the Daggerford region, Aldrine Lugar, a sailor who had been washed over the side of her vessel during a storm, awoke on the beach of a small rocky island. The island afforded very little aside from grasses and scrub bushes, and even less in the food department. Tiny blueberries were the only edible things, and within a couple of days she had finished eating the meager amount that she could scavenge. The only other creatures on the island were the colorful, dancing butterflies, and to the shipwrecked sailor, the butterfly symbolized freedom at being able to fly away from her imprisoning predicament. Resigned to her fate of starvation on this miserable rock, Aldrine waited for the inevitable. However, something large and purple floated ashore overnight, and it spelled freedom: a gigantic gourd! She had heard stories of such things existing in the infamous Lizard Marsh, and this one must surely have been swept out to sea from there. There was still a cork wedged into the spout, which must have prevented it sinking on its long voyage. Using her knife to carve the name "Butterfly" onto the side of her newly discovered craft, Aldrine then lashed herself securely to the gourd with vines and set out to sea. Umberlee's malicious attentions must have been turned elsewhere, for it is said the sailor found herself not far from the mouth of the River Delimbiyr but three days later. Riding a giant gourd on the rough waves of the Sea of Swords can't be called the most comfortable of trips, but it's definitely better than passing away among the butterflies.

This stuffed parrot sits motionless upon its perch, head cocked to one side as if waiting attentively for what you'll say next. A small, crinkled note dangles on a string attached to one of its claws: "Poor Polly! She mimicked the captain one too many times. May she perch in peace."

During one of the bloody wars with the hordes from Dragonspear Castle, the army banner of the Daggerford militia was lost as militia forces retreated to regroup closer to Daggerford. The orcs and other devilish creatures brought the banner back to Dragonspear Castle amidst much reveling, where they propped it up on the top of the tallest tower as a trophy. The castle, which was crawling with thousands of orcs (and worse) was impregnable. The life expectancy of a rat inside that horrible place was considered to be under a minute. With his militia demoralized, the Duke of Daggerford knew that the only way to prevent a crushing defeat was to recover the army's banner. Yet such a task seemed impossible. Despite the suicidal odds, and to everyone's surprise, one militia soldier immediately stepped forward to the challenge. Kaylet Wespil had never been known to be the heroic type. She did her duty as best she could, but shied away from risky missions that forged heroes; that had been something her father, a famous hero for hire, had excelled at. However, she did have one thing in her favor: she knew of a way into Dragonspear Castle that would allow her to take the banner right from under the noses of the orcs. Striding out of the duke's field tent after volunteering, she immediately rode to her small stone cottage several miles away. Opening a small box that had been kept by her father, she found the object she was looking for: a small magical whistle. An hour after blowing it, a gigantic shadow loomed over her cottage and across her awestruck face. Later that same day, Kaylet re-entered her leader's tent and unfurled the army banner of Daggerford before an astounded duke. "How?!" was all he could bring himself to say. She brought him to his tent door and pointed outside. Before him stood a mighty bronze dragon, flexing its wings before a group of astonished militia. "I've called in an old debt to me father," she explained. "It didn't take much to fly to Dragonspear Castle, swoop down to the tallest tower, and quickly snatch the banner. The stupid orcs probably didn't even know what had happened until after we'd left." So impressed was the duke, that he commissioned the dragon to fight alongside his army. At their next battle, it was the orc rabble's turn to flee, and be subsequently cut down by the Daggerford cavalry.

Sculpted by the "almost famous" local sculptor, Yujist Glemp, this statue was presented as a gift to the good people of Gillian's Hill. Despite the benefactive gesture, folk around the hamlet couldn't help but notice that the statue looked an awful lot like Glemp himself! So it came as no surprise that late one night, someone decided to do a little sculpting refinement of their own. Yujist was enraged when he saw the result, and stormed about Gillian's Hill in search of the culprit, whom he never discovered. It had been his intent to re-bestow yet another masterpiece unto his deprived fans ("those ungrateful peasants" as he endearingly put it). This time, however, it was to be a gold casting of himself mounted upon an obelisk...a very tall obelisk, with a very "out of reach of their barbarous chisels" casting. Unfortunately, Yujist disappeared not long after this incident, before his new masterpiece was even started, and the embarrassing statue was moved to somewhere where decent folk wouldn't have to look at it.

Deep beneath Gillian's Hill lies an ancient tomb, as old as Netheril, or perhaps older. It was pillaged long ago from the Underdark below, and was even used as a base at one point by a band of illithids, that controlled the minds of Trade Way travelers, luring them to a mindless doom into the tomb. The tomb itself can only be entered through an invisible portal, the location of which is practically impossible to find. The last group of adventurers who did manage to find it, returned from the depths carrying this strange item, undoubtedly a leftover from the time of the illithids. None of the adventurers (all of whom were fighters and barbarians) were able to figure out what a crystal on a bouncy spring actually did, and so, deeming it worthless, they sold it to Torleth for a few gold pieces. Torleth keeps it around for the kiddies, who enjoy bouncing on the curious contraption. The illithids would be horrified.

This plate of food has been heavily lacquered in order to preserve it. It is said that this was the famous final meal of Lady Franchilsa III, although it remained uneaten. She adamantly declared it to be poisoned and, pushing it aside, strode out of the dining hall and into the palace gardens for some air, where she met her untimely end in a chance encounter with an escaped circus lion. The meal, which was confirmed to contain not less than 23 poisons, was kept by her son afterwards as proof of a secret plot against his mother, to be used at a possible later inquiry, which never came. Still, the untouched final meal of Lady Franchilsa III would go down in history as the deadliest meal that was never eaten. If one counts the heavy lacquer, there are now 24 deadly poisons upon the food. Best not to even touch it.

The sling earned its nickname during an altercation with an arcane archer who pursued the monk through a series of shadowy catacombs. After a lengthy chase, Silence feared the archer had him cornered. So he aimed the sling at the archer's slow-moving silhouette and fired with all the strength he could muster. The sling bullet careened off the stone wall and bounced its way down the hall, eventually striking the archer squarely in the chest.

Stunned from the direct assault to his shallow breastplate, the archer let his guard down for but a moment. Silence closed in and quickly subdued the archer with a blazing flurry of well-placed punches and roundhouse kicks.

This appears to be the journal of the temple of Bhaal's high priest. Most of the book details the gruesome ritual activities of the clergy over a number of years leading up to the Time of Troubles. Only the last few entries seem to be of interest:

13 Ches, 1358
A public sacrifice to Bhaal has increased the religious fervor of the faithful. The woman was burned in the town square under the guise of a witch. Her screams of torment may even find her a place in the afterlife.

25 Ches, 1358
I was required to trim our order as a traitor was amongst us, so says the messenger of Bhaal. Our blood pools are restocked and at least four faithful have moved on to their rewards. Regardless of whether we have actually trimmed the traitor from our midst, the display was poignant.

4 Tarsakh, 1358
It has been a night blessed by Bhaal. We returned with five children, all of which shall please Bhaal in various fashions. The morning light broke with screams reaching our ears. Yes, blessed be Bhaal!

16 Eleint, 1358
The mass was interrupted this eve by an invading force of humans, elves, and animals, who all exuded the disgusting stench of nature. These infidels caused considerable damage to the inner temple walls, and killed several priests before we repelled them. Bhaal shall require much satiating for this affront. We will take revenge upon these intruders, but first, I must find an appropriate sacrifice.

17 Eleint, 1358
As if the previous night's sacrilege against Bhaal was not enough, this morning has brought more misfortune. Something truly perplexing has occurred. It is as if Bhaal's gaze upon us has simply vanished, as he no longer answers our prayers. I am at a loss to explain this and the ritual sacrifice done thrice over appears not to have helped matters. We have sent word to the temple in Waterdeep in search of an explanation. In the meantime, I have safely secured all of the temple's most precious treasures in the secret vault. Hopefully an answer to this mystery is forthcoming...

This is the journal's final entry, followed by blank pages until the end of the book.

The Treatise of Suffering
Author: Unknown

Life is pain. The suffering begins at childbirth and ends when we gasp our final breath. As disciples in Bhaal's order, it is our duty to remind the heathens that pain is the essence of life and provides the only true path to salvation.

Cries of agony ring like musical notes in the ears of our Dread Lord. The cries of children, in particular, provide our Master with great joy for they represent anguish in its purest form, freed from the bonds of duty and convention. Each time a child cries out in pain, our Master feels a sensation akin to rapture.

As shepherds in the service of Bhaal, it is our sworn duty to see that the cries of the living reach our Master's ears. At times, this may involve intensifying or prolonging the suffering of our "flock." Bhaal has decreed that the reward for our dutiful service shall be nothing less than a life free of pain, except for that issued at Bhaal's command.

For those disciples who have mistakenly allied themselves against Bhaal's plan for salvation, there is no recourse but pain, administered at its highest threshold. We must let their cries ring out loud and long, so our Master may channel misery into bliss.

Life is pain. All praise the Lord of Murder!

The Bakadi Brothers, Jemzo and Jamzo, were two of the finest thieves ever to emerge from the sweltering streets of Memnon in faraway Calimshan. Their bravery and cunning were the stuff of legend even within their own lifetimes, and they rose rapidly to head one of the infamous crime cartels of their homeland.

It was said that "no job was too big, no vault too well protected, and no maiden able to resist" the power of the Bakadi brothers, but it seems that this was somewhat of an exaggeration. A little over 400 years ago they left their homes, telling trusted lieutenants they were 'heading out for the greatest heist of all time'. They were never seen again.

The presence of their remains here suggest that the aforesaid 'heist' involved the treasures of the wizard and warrior Sundar Halyndliam, and clearly they were unsuccessful. Exactly what he did with them upon their capture is unclear, but their skulls are now potent in magic, and clearly have been tampered with by someone with great knowledge of the arcane.

Eye Scream

Ingredients:

2 tbsp. eye of newt
2 cups swamp water (brackish)
1/2 cup blueberries
3 cups Gorgon's milk (substitute cow's milk if Gorgon's is not available)
1 cup good intentions (or other sugary sweetener)

Directions:

1. In a medium bronze cauldron, reduce eye of newt, blueberries, and swamp water to a sludge-like consistency.
2. Over a low fire, slowly mix in good intentions while stirring vigorously with a holly branch so mixture doesn't burn.
3. Remove cauldron from heat and slowly stir in milk. 
4. Cast a Ray of Frost spell on the cauldron and serve!

A wise king had this crown commissioned when he rightly surmised that his advisors were plotting against him. Secretly substituting this crown for the one attained at his coronation, he eventually was able to discover and capture the treasonous aides. This eventually led the "fake" crown to supplant the original as the symbol of rulership.

It is ironic, then, how a traveling bard managed to return the original crown to its rightful place. Sneaking about the castle the night before her performance, the bard managed to swap crowns, placing the fake in the castle vault and the original on the king's nightstand. The next night, after giving the performance of her life, the bard was told she could claim whatever she liked from the king's treasury. She claimed the crown from the vault for her own, unbeknownst to all as being the fake, and was never seen again...

This worn and weather-beaten tome has had all but the very last entry torn out, as if the author intentionally destroyed all record of their prior thoughts or achievements. The final entry is written in a hurried, erratic fashion, which might call into question the author's sanity:

Fifteen years ago, when I finalized my doctrine on Theorosophy, I never dreamed it would morph into the abomination that now plagues me so. The initial concept was sound: that one should not discount deep, psychic urges and the motivations of the unconscious mind when attempting to validate an unproven hypothesis. Too often, science ignores a creature's base, primeval desires, and instead chooses to place too much importance on facts and clinical data.

Where I went wrong was in my attempts to translate this new approach to my pupils, a couple of fawning, inept university rejects named Beb-Shuur and Xianga. These two brainless nitwits seem less concerned with the "meaning" of my words than with the syntax. For example, although I desired to apply more weight to emotions and ideals, they've chosen to do so by forsaking the primary intent of philosophical theory, which is to prove a hypothesis using factual data.

Instead, the blathering idiots use empiricism simply to bolster their twisted, quasi-spiritual view of the world and have begun promoting this new pseudo-science in all the trade journals. Worse still, they've named me as their mentor, which has drastically reduced my standing within the philosophical community.

My reputation is in tatters and without that, I am nothing...

Lieutenant Skron kept a logbook detailing the Zhentarim's caravan raids along the Tradeway. The last few entries are as follows.

Faern & Young, from Scornubel - Silver and wine shipment.  Killed the guards and Young, enslaved Faern.

Boldug and Co. - Acquired shipment of furs and leathers. Convinced the cart driver it was in his best interest to join the Black Network trading branch.

Chessbalad Trading - A shipment of pots and jars not worth our time. Robbed cart driver instead.

Urgand Sisters Emporium - Ambushed one of our own caravans by mistake! We all had a good laugh. Captain Dratharion wasn't laughing though. Said I'd end up as Bugo's toilet scrubber if it happened again.

Calim's Exquisite Wares - Raiding party was set to take this shipment of gold, but the party mysteriously didn't return. Might be linked to that hero who helped those farmers.
